methodological_rigor.justification: This is a large single-center retrospective cohort of 650 women undergoing elective surgery for histologically confirmed endometrial cancer (2020–2025), comparing four perioperative analgesia strategies with clinically relevant co-primary outcomes (LOS >7 days and Clavien–Dindo grade II+ complications). The design is appropriate for evaluating associations in routine practice and the manuscript reports multivariable logistic regression and linear mixed-effects models to adjust for confounding, along with subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Key limitations are inherent to non-randomized exposure assignment and potential unmeasured confounders; the authors also note reliance on scheduled medication records for group assignment and restriction to in-hospital outcomes due to incomplete post-discharge follow-up.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort study evaluating postoperative outcomes by analgesia modality, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is high because opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia directly affects pain, nausea/vomiting, mobilization, and complications after cancer surgery, and the study reports better outcomes in multimodal/regional groups (e.g., lower POD1 pain scores, lower PONV, shorter mean LOS, and lower complication incidence). The adjusted analyses indicate multimodal analgesia is independently associated with reduced prolonged hospitalization (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.31–0.87) and complications (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.30–0.99), which could inform perioperative pathway design.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE applies to this retrospective cohort, and the manuscript clearly defines exposure groups, outcomes (including Clavien–Dindo grading), and modeling approaches (logistic regression, linear mixed-effects), with quantitative effect estimates and subgroup analyses. The limitations section appropriately discusses confounding, potential exposure misclassification, single-center external validity, and lack of consistent 30-day follow-up. The manuscript does not describe deposition of patient-level data or analysis code, so reproducibility is limited outside the source EMR.

novelty_literature.justification: Multimodal analgesia is a well-established perioperative concept, so the work is not conceptually novel; its contribution is applying a four-arm regimen classification in a disease-specific endometrial cancer surgical cohort at scale (n=650). The inclusion of immune-inflammatory markers (NLR, CRP) as secondary endpoints and modeling them longitudinally adds incremental mechanistic context. Overall this is a meaningful, practice-adjacent extension rather than a paradigm shift.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly structured with explicit definitions of analgesia groups, primary/secondary outcomes, and statistical methods, and the abstract reports key numerical findings (e.g., NRS pain differences, PONV rates, LOS, and adjusted ORs). The limitations are written plainly and match the design constraints (retrospective, single-center, in-hospital outcomes). Figure/table captions enumerate the major analyses (baseline characteristics, regression models, subgroup/sensitivity tables), which supports readability even in the normalized format.

key_strengths: Large real-world cohort (n=650) with clinically meaningful outcomes (LOS >7 days, Clavien–Dindo grade II+ complications) and multiple recovery endpoints (pain, PONV, ambulation/flatus).
Uses adjusted models (logistic regression and linear mixed-effects) and reports effect sizes for multimodal analgesia (e.g., OR 0.52 for prolonged LOS and OR 0.55 for complications).
Includes subgroup and sensitivity analyses and integrates perioperative inflammatory markers (NLR, CRP) to support biological plausibility.
key_concerns: Retrospective, non-randomized assignment of analgesia strategy leaves room for unmeasured confounding despite adjustment.
Exposure classification based on scheduled medication records may miss meaningful intraoperative/postoperative variations in practice and adherence.
Outcomes are limited to in-hospital events due to inconsistent standardized post-discharge follow-up, potentially undercounting complications/readmissions.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The study is well executed for a retrospective design and the effect sizes are clinically relevant, but tier-2 acceptance would likely require stronger confounding control/causal framing and more complete follow-up capture beyond hospitalization.
